# Hours, Output and the Pilot Problem: A Re-examination of the Halden Reduced-Hours Pilot

*Comment, Journal of Labour and Organisation Studies. K. Varga and T. Holm, Centre for Applied Labour Statistics.*

## Abstract

The Halden pilot reported that 61 organisations maintained output while cutting scheduled hours by 20%, implying a 23.4% gain in output per hour. Using the pilot's microdata, released under the Institute's data-sharing policy, we re-examine the result. Four problems, each documented below, account for most of the reported gain: attrition that was not random, a manager-reported output measure that overstates output relative to organisations' own records, an hours denominator that counts scheduled rather than actual time, and an unadjusted revenue comparison. Correcting the first three, the gain in output per hour falls from 23.4% to 10.8% in the subset of organisations where correction is possible. We then argue that the remaining gain is plausibly a novelty effect, and that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty.

## 1. Attrition

The working paper states that nine of the 70 enrolled organisations "withdrew during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons". The microdata tell a different story. Seven of the nine withdrew after the reduced schedule had begun: four in the first month and three in the second. In exit forms, six of the nine gave workload or inability to maintain output as the main reason, and two gave scheduling. The organisations that found the change hardest were therefore removed from the sample before the outcome was measured. With nine of 70 organisations missing, and those nine plausibly the least successful, the reported sample of 61 is a sample of survivors.

## 2. The output measure

The primary outcome was an index completed by a manager who was also the pilot's internal sponsor. Managers were asked to base the index on organisational records, but were not required to submit them. Twenty-three organisations did submit underlying records (billable hours delivered, tickets closed, units produced, or cases completed). For these 23 we can compare the manager's index with the index implied by the records.

**Table 1. Manager-reported and record-based output, 23 organisations with records**

| Measure | Mean output index (baseline = 100) |
|---|---|
| Manager-reported index | 98.9 |
| Index computed from submitted records | 95.1 |
| Difference | −3.8 points |

In 19 of the 23 organisations the manager-reported index exceeded the record-based index. We do not suggest bad faith. A manager responsible for a change he or she advocated, asked to rate its effect on a scale where 100 means "unchanged", will tend to round toward success. But the difference is systematic, and the headline output figure of 98.7 should not be taken at face value.

## 3. The hours denominator

The pilot computed output per hour by dividing output by the ratio of scheduled hours, 0.8. Twenty-seven organisations used time-tracking software throughout. Their data show average actual weekly hours of 40.3 at baseline and 34.6 during the pilot, a fall of 14.1% rather than 20%. The difference comes from two sources visible in the logs: longer working days on the remaining four days (average +0.7 hours per day), and work logged on the scheduled day off (on average 1.6 hours per week). Some further work on the day off is probably not logged.

Seventeen organisations have both submitted output records and time tracking. In this subset, record-based output was 95.4 and actual hours fell from 40.4 to 34.8 (−13.9%). The implied gain in output per actual hour is 10.8% (95.4 / 86.1), less than half the reported 23.4%.

**Table 2. Implied gain in output per hour under successive corrections**

| Specification | Output | Hours ratio | Gain per hour |
|---|---|---|---|
| As reported (all 61) | 98.7 | 0.800 | +23.4% |
| Record-based output, scheduled hours (23) | 95.1 | 0.800 | +18.9% |
| Manager-reported output, actual hours (27) | 98.4 | 0.859 | +14.6% |
| Record-based output, actual hours (17) | 95.4 | 0.861 | +10.8% |

## 4. Revenue

The working paper reports revenue 1.4% higher than in the previous year. This is a nominal comparison. Consumer prices rose by 4.1% over the same twelve months; in real terms, revenue in participating organisations fell by approximately 2.6%. Revenue is in any case a poor proxy for productivity, but the figure as presented gives a misleading impression of growth.

## 5. Sectoral claims

The pilot concluded that gains in output per hour were "found in every sector" and that the model is "sector-general". This conclusion is an artifact of the per-hour metric. When hours are cut by 20%, any output index above 80 will register as a per-hour gain. Retail and hospitality output fell by 6.9% on the manager-reported measure; the three retail and hospitality organisations among the 23 with records show a fall of 11.2%. A fall in output of this size in a customer-facing business is not evidence that reduced hours work there. The Varden County trial's counter and contact-centre stratum, the only randomised evidence on coverage-bound work, found a fall in output per employee of 11.4% and longer waits for the public. That is, in our view, the most reliable finding in the literature to date.

## 6. Novelty

After the corrections above, a gain in output per actual hour of about 11% remains in the subset of survivors with usable data. We think this residual should not be read as a durable effect. The pilot's own survey shows self-reported energy at work rising by 0.61 standard deviations at month three and falling to 0.29 at month six. Extrapolating this decline, energy would return to baseline at around month ten. A change that staff chose, welcomed and knew to be under evaluation is the classic setting for a novelty effect: effort rises while the change is new and observed, and falls back once it is routine. Six months is not long enough to distinguish a novelty effect from a durable one, and the burden of proof lies with those claiming the latter.

## 7. The meetings hypothesis

The Varden trial's authors report, in an unregistered exploratory analysis, that cuts in recurring meetings correlated with per-hour gains across seven treated offices, and suggest this as a mechanism. We regard this as a post hoc account fitted to a subgroup. A correlation across seven offices, selected for analysis after the results were known, is precisely the kind of finding that does not replicate. The meetings explanation has an intuitive appeal that has outrun its evidence, and it should not be cited as a mechanism.

## 8. Conclusion

Taking the problems together: attrition removed the organisations least able to cope; the output measure overstated output by roughly four points; the hours measure overstated the reduction in time by roughly six points; and the remaining gain coincides with a decaying measure of enthusiasm. We conclude that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the best-supported finding is the negative one: where output depends on presence, reduced hours reduce output.

We recommend that future evaluations use record-based output, actual hours, a randomised or at least matched comparison group, follow-up of at least eighteen months, and analysis of all enrolled organisations including those that withdraw.

## Data note

All re-analyses use the Halden pilot microdata (release 1.2). The corrections in Table 2 can only be computed for subsets of organisations, and those subsets were not chosen at random; organisations with time tracking and records may differ from the others. Our corrected estimates therefore describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole.

# Review: "Hours, Output and the Pilot Problem" (Varga & Holm, comment)

The comment's re-analysis (sections 1–5) is valuable and mostly sound. It uses the microdata to confirm, and put numbers on, several concerns about the Halden paper, including some raised in the earlier reviews. The interpretive sections (6–8) overreach. The headline conclusion that per-hour gains are "entirely an artifact" does not follow from the comment's own estimates, and it ignores the strongest evidence against it, from the same Varden trial the comment cites approvingly.

Most of the arithmetic checks out:
- Table 2: 95.1/0.8 = +18.9%; 98.4/0.859 = +14.6%; 95.4/0.861 = +10.8%.
- Hours: 34.6/40.3 = 0.859 (−14.1%); 34.8/40.4 = 0.861 (−13.9%).
- Revenue: 1.014/1.041 = 0.974, a real fall of about 2.6%.

The exceptions are in points 2 and 6 below.

## What the comment gets right

- **Attrition.** If the microdata are as described, this is the most serious finding. Seven of the nine withdrawals happened *after* the reduced schedule began, and six gave workload or output as the main reason. The working paper's account ("during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons") would then be inaccurate, not just incomplete. The Halden authors should be asked to respond.
- **The output measure.** Manager indices exceeded record-based indices in 19 of 23 organisations, by 3.8 points on average. This is direct evidence of the rater bias the working paper only listed as a limitation.
- **Revenue.** Deflating it is correct.
- **Sectoral claims.** The point that any index above 80 registers as a per-hour gain is correct, as is reading retail and hospitality as negative evidence. The three-organisation retail figure (−11.2%) is very small, though, and should be presented as illustrative.
- **The data note.** It honestly states that the corrected estimates describe non-random subsets.

## 1. The abstract misdescribes the correction

The abstract says "correcting the first three" problems (attrition, output measure, hours) brings the gain to 10.8%. Table 2 corrects only output and hours. Attrition is described in section 1 but never corrected or bounded.

Seven of the nine withdrawing organisations ran the schedule for one to two months, so they may have early monthly indices. Even a worst-case bound, such as assigning them the lowest observed outcomes, would be more informative than leaving attrition unquantified. The abstract should be corrected either way.

## 2. The hours decomposition doesn't add up

Section 3 attributes the gap between scheduled and actual hours to two sources:

- +0.7 hours on each of four remaining days = 2.8 hours
- 1.6 hours logged on the day off
- Total: 4.4 hours above the 32-hour schedule, which implies about 36.4 hours per week

The reported pilot average is 34.6, only 2.6 hours above schedule. Either a component is misstated or the average is. This matters:
- At 36.4 actual hours, the fall in hours is about 10%, not 14%.
- The per-hour gain would then shrink further, to roughly 6% on record-based output.

So the error could cut in the comment's favour, but it needs resolving before the figures are relied on.

## 3. Table 2 changes the sample along with the correction

Each row uses a different set of organisations: 61, 23, 27 and 17. The fall from 23.4% to 10.8% therefore mixes the effect of the corrections with differences in which organisations are included.

The 17 organisations with both records and time tracking may lean towards sectors where both are routine, such as software and professional services. A cleaner presentation would apply all four specifications to the *same* 17 organisations, so the effect of each correction can be read directly.

No confidence intervals are reported anywhere. An estimate from 17 organisations should have one.

## 4. The novelty argument is the weakest part, and it carries the conclusion

After correction, a gain of about 11% remains. The comment attributes all of it to novelty on this basis:

- **Wrong outcome.** The evidence is self-reported *energy*, not output. The comment shows no link between the decline in energy and any decline in productivity.
- **Two-point extrapolation.** The trend is fitted to two data points (+0.61 SD at month three, +0.29 at month six). A rise followed by a plateau fits them equally well.
- **Arithmetic.** Even taking the linear extrapolation at face value, the line reaches zero at about month 8.7, not "around month ten". This is minor, but it is unexplained.
- **The direct test was available and not run.** The Halden output index was collected *monthly*, and the comment's authors have the microdata. If novelty drives the gain, per-hour output should decline from month three to month six. Checking that would have been decisive, and its absence is the main gap in the comment.

The appeal to the "burden of proof" doesn't substitute for this. A novelty effect is a hypothesis like any other, and the comment presents it as the default without evidence on output.

## 5. Selective use of the Varden trial

The comment calls the Varden counter-stratum result "the most reliable finding in the literature" but does not mention the case-processing stratum of the same trial. That stratum found:
- output per FTE of −2.1% (CI −6.8 to +2.6) relative to control;
- **+12.5% output per actual hour (CI +6.9 to +18.4).**

That estimate was obtained with record-based output, timesheet hours and randomisation. These address exactly the measurement and selection problems the comment identifies, and the trial ran for nine months, longer than the Halden pilot. The comment's own standards therefore make it the strongest evidence of a real per-hour gain in non-coverage work.

A conclusion that such gains are "entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty" can't stand while this result goes unaddressed. At most, the comment can argue that novelty has not been ruled out beyond nine months. The Varden 24-month follow-up is the proper test of that.

## 6. The meetings critique is partly a straw man and applies uneven standards

- **Already caveated.** The Varden authors already labelled the meetings analysis unregistered, said a correlation across seven offices "cannot establish a mechanism", and registered a confirmatory test. The comment's objections largely repeat their caveats while implying the authors overclaimed.
- **"Selected after the results were known."** This isn't supported. The meeting data were collected in month six at managers' request, before the nine-month results.
- **Uneven standards.** The comment rejects a caveated seven-office correlation as unfit to cite, yet relies on a two-point extrapolation of a self-report measure to explain away the entire residual gain. Novelty and meeting reduction are competing explanations, and they make different predictions about persistence. Neither has been tested, and the comment should treat them alike.

## 7. The conclusion contradicts the data note

The data note says the corrected estimates "describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole". The conclusion then generalises beyond the pilot to "reduced-hours schemes" in general. A defensible conclusion would say:

> In the Halden subsets with usable data, correcting output and hours reduces the implied per-hour gain from 23% to about 11% (before addressing attrition). Whether the remainder persists is untested. Where output depends on presence, reduced hours reduce output.

That is still a strong and useful critique. The "entirely an artifact" claim should be removed from both the abstract and the conclusion.

## Smaller points

- **Unsourced inflation figure.** The CPI figure (4.1%) needs a source and should match the period of the revenue comparison. A producer-price or sector deflator may also suit business revenue better than consumer prices.
- **Unclear output measure.** In section 5, "6.9% on the manager-reported measure" refers to the full retail sample, while "11.2%" refers to three organisations. Labelling these clearly would avoid the impression of a like-for-like comparison.
- **Recommendations.** These are sound and consistent with the Varden design. Eighteen-month follow-up is reasonable, and analysis of all enrolled organisations is important given section 1.

## Overall

Sections 1–5 should be published. They correct the Halden record on attrition, output measurement, hours and revenue. Sections 6–8 need substantial revision:
- test novelty directly using the monthly output data;
- engage with the Varden case-processing result;
- apply the same evidential standard to novelty as to the meetings hypothesis;
- limit the conclusion to what the corrected subsets can support.
